options.a: Instruct overnight fasting per protocol
options.b: Tell the patient to stop all medications that day
options.c: Allow coffee with cream before the morning draw
options.d: Ask the patient to fast for 4 hours, with water

distractorExplanations.b: Patients usually keep taking prescribed medications unless the provider says otherwise; fasting means no food or caloric drinks.
distractorExplanations.c: Cream and sugar add fat and calories that break the fast; only water is allowed before a fasting lipid draw.
distractorExplanations.d: A fasting lipid panel typically needs 9 to 12 hours without food; 4 hours is too short to count as fasting.

amt-rma-readiness-check-clinical-001.explanation: Fasting labs require clear preparation instructions to avoid invalid results and repeat visits; confirm the patient understands the instructions.

options.a: Review documentation and payer policy, then appeal
options.b: Resubmit the same claim unchanged and wait for payment
options.c: Change the diagnosis code to one that pays
options.d: Bill the patient for the full amount at once

distractorExplanations.b: Resubmitting an unchanged claim usually triggers the same denial; the medical-necessity issue must be reviewed first.
distractorExplanations.c: Changing codes without documentation support is fraud.
distractorExplanations.d: Billing the patient before reviewing the denial and appeal rights is premature and may be prohibited.

options.a: Guarantee that Medicare pays for the service
options.b: Replace informed consent for a procedure
options.c: Warn that Medicare may not pay for a service
options.d: Enroll the patient in a Medicare plan

distractorExplanations.a: An ABN warns of possible denial; it guarantees nothing.
distractorExplanations.b: Informed consent is separate and still required.
distractorExplanations.d: Plan enrollment is handled through Medicare, not an ABN.

options.a: Active dates, plan type, and referral needs
options.b: The patient's employer and job title
options.c: The patient's preferred pharmacy and appointment times
options.d: The patient's past medical history

distractorExplanations.c: Pharmacy and scheduling preferences are registration details; they do not confirm active coverage or referral rules.
distractorExplanations.b: Employer details may be on file but do not confirm coverage.
distractorExplanations.d: Medical history is clinical intake, not insurance verification.

options.a: Capture diagnoses and services for billing
options.b: Serve as a prescription pad for controlled substances
options.c: Record the patient's consent to treatment
options.d: Itemize the remittance advice sent by the payer

distractorExplanations.c: Consent to treatment is a separate signed form; the superbill lists the codes and charges for the visit.
distractorExplanations.d: The remittance advice comes from the payer after adjudication; the superbill is created at the visit, before the claim.
distractorExplanations.b: It is not a controlled-substance prescription form.

amt-rma-readiness-check-clinical-007.explanation: Superbills list common diagnoses/procedures to support charge capture for the encounter; they capture billing data from the visit.

options.a: Strike once; initial, date, and correct it
options.b: Cover the error with correction fluid
options.c: Remove the page and rewrite the entire entry
options.d: Write over the error until unreadable

distractorExplanations.c: Removing or replacing a page destroys part of the legal record and looks like tampering, even if rewritten neatly.
distractorExplanations.b: Correction fluid hides the original entry, which is not allowed.
distractorExplanations.d: Obliterating the original entry makes the record look altered.

options.a: A patient pays cash for an office visit
options.b: A patient requests a copy of their records
options.c: A patient schedules an annual Medicare wellness visit
options.d: A payer requires approval before covering a service

distractorExplanations.c: Medicare's annual wellness visit is a covered preventive service that generally needs no prior authorization.
distractorExplanations.a: Cash payment involves no payer, so no authorization is needed.
distractorExplanations.b: Records requests fall under HIPAA access rules, not payer approval.

options.a: PPO plans require a PCP referral for every specialist visit
options.b: A referral means the payer has approved payment in full
options.c: Many HMO plans require referrals before specialty care
options.d: Original Medicare requires a referral for each specialist

distractorExplanations.a: PPOs typically let members see in-network specialists without a referral; that confuses PPO rules with HMO rules.
distractorExplanations.b: A referral directs care but is not a payment guarantee or prior authorization; the claim can still be denied.
distractorExplanations.d: Original Medicare has no referral requirement for specialists; many Medicare Advantage HMOs do require one.

amt-rma-readiness-check-clinical-012.explanation: Managed care plans often require referrals or authorizations for specialty services; HMO plans are the classic example.

options.a: 100°C (212°F) at normal pressure for 5 minutes
options.b: 70°C (158°F) with alcohol vapor for 10 minutes
options.c: 121°C (250°F) at about 15 psi for 15–30 minutes
options.d: 160°C (320°F) in dry heat for about 15 minutes

distractorExplanations.d: Dry-heat sterilization at 160°C needs about 2 hours; 15 minutes confuses dry heat with steam cycle times.
distractorExplanations.a: Boiling at normal pressure does not reliably kill bacterial spores.
distractorExplanations.b: Alcohol is a disinfectant, not a sterilizing method for instruments.

options.a: Toward the midline of the body
options.b: Closer to the trunk or point of origin
options.c: Toward the front of the body
options.d: Farther from the trunk or point of origin

distractorExplanations.a: Moving toward the midline of the body is the definition of medial, not proximal.
distractorExplanations.c: Toward the front of the body is anterior (ventral); proximal refers to nearness to the trunk or origin.
distractorExplanations.d: That defines distal.

options.a: Hypokalemia
options.b: Hypocalcemia
options.c: Hyponatremia
options.d: Hyperkalemia

distractorExplanations.a: Hypokalemia more often causes U waves/flattened T waves.
distractorExplanations.b: Hypocalcemia affects QT interval differently.
distractorExplanations.c: Sodium disorders have different presentations.

options.a: Intramuscularly into the mid-outer thigh
options.b: Subcutaneously into the back of the upper arm
options.c: Intravenously by the patient at home
options.d: Sublingually as a tablet dissolved under the tongue

distractorExplanations.b: Auto-injectors are designed for IM delivery into the thigh; subcutaneous arm injection absorbs more slowly.
distractorExplanations.d: No sublingual epinephrine tablet is the standard anaphylaxis rescue; auto-injectors deliver it intramuscularly.
distractorExplanations.c: Patients do not self-administer IV epinephrine at home.

options.a: Procedures and services performed
options.b: Diagnoses and reasons for encounter
options.c: Drugs, supplies, and equipment
options.d: The place where the service was performed

distractorExplanations.d: Where the service took place is reported with place-of-service codes, not ICD-10-CM diagnosis codes.
distractorExplanations.a: Procedures and services are reported with CPT.
distractorExplanations.c: Drugs, supplies, and equipment are HCPCS Level II.

options.a: Diagnoses and reasons for the encounter
options.b: Drugs, supplies, and durable equipment
options.c: Procedures and services performed
options.d: The place-of-service location

distractorExplanations.a: Diagnoses and encounter reasons are reported with ICD-10-CM codes, not CPT codes.
distractorExplanations.b: Drugs, supplies and durable medical equipment are reported with HCPCS Level II codes, not CPT.
distractorExplanations.d: The setting of care is reported with two-digit place-of-service codes on the claim, not with CPT.

options.a: Before touching a patient for a routine exam
options.b: After removing gloves when hands look clean
options.c: Before putting on sterile gloves for a dressing change
options.d: Hands visibly soiled or after C. difficile care

distractorExplanations.c: Alcohol rub is acceptable before donning sterile gloves for a clinical procedure when hands are not soiled.
distractorExplanations.a: Alcohol rub is appropriate before routine patient contact when hands are not soiled.
distractorExplanations.b: Alcohol rub is acceptable after glove removal if hands are not visibly soiled.

options.a: Measure the total urine volume over 24 hours
options.b: Let the patient avoid cleansing before collection
options.c: Collect the most concentrated first-morning urine
options.d: Minimize contamination from skin and genital flora

distractorExplanations.a: Total volume requires a timed 24-hour collection.
distractorExplanations.b: Cleansing is a required step of a clean catch.
distractorExplanations.c: First-morning specimens are about concentration, not contamination control.

options.a: The center tip of the index finger, along the prints
options.b: The side of the thumb near the nail
options.c: The medial or lateral plantar heel surface
options.d: Palmar middle or ring finger, slightly off-center

distractorExplanations.a: The index fingertip is more sensitive and callused, the tip is near bone, and cutting along the prints lets blood run.
distractorExplanations.b: The thumb has a pulse and thicker tissue and is not recommended.
distractorExplanations.c: Heel sticks are used for infants, not adults.

options.a: Gastric mucosa
options.b: Esophagus
options.c: Large intestine
options.d: Small intestine

distractorExplanations.a: The stomach lining mixes and starts digesting food but absorbs little besides some water, alcohol and certain drugs.
distractorExplanations.b: The esophagus only transports food to the stomach.
distractorExplanations.c: The large intestine absorbs mainly water and electrolytes.

options.a: Lavender-top (EDTA) tube
options.b: Gray-top (sodium fluoride/potassium oxalate) tube
options.c: Blood culture bottles or sterile tubes
options.d: Light-blue-top (sodium citrate) tube

distractorExplanations.b: Gray-top fluoride/oxalate tubes are drawn last in the CLSI order, after lavender EDTA tubes.
distractorExplanations.d: Citrate tubes come first only when no blood cultures are ordered; sterile culture bottles precede them.
distractorExplanations.a: EDTA comes near the end; drawn early, its carryover can falsely raise potassium and lower calcium in later tubes.

options.a: Documenting vital signs accurately
options.b: Performing a procedure after valid informed consent
options.c: Threatening to restrain a patient who refuses care
options.d: Touching or treating a patient without consent

distractorExplanations.c: A threat that creates fear of contact is assault; battery requires actual unauthorized touching.
distractorExplanations.a: Accurate documentation is appropriate.
distractorExplanations.b: Consented care is not battery.

options.a: Only patients with known infections pose a risk
options.b: Any patient's blood or body fluids may be infectious
options.c: Wearing gloves replaces the need for hand hygiene afterward
options.d: Patients without symptoms need no special precautions

distractorExplanations.d: People without symptoms can still carry bloodborne pathogens, so precautions apply to every patient.
distractorExplanations.c: Gloves can have defects and hands get contaminated during removal, so hand hygiene is still required afterward.
distractorExplanations.a: Standard Precautions apply to every patient, not only known infections.

options.a: Reasonable emergency aid given in good faith
options.b: Care given as part of a paid clinic shift
options.c: Grossly negligent care given at an accident
options.d: Emergency care given in exchange for payment

distractorExplanations.b: Care within a paid job carries a duty to treat and is outside Good Samaritan protection.
distractorExplanations.c: Gross negligence and willful misconduct are generally not protected.
distractorExplanations.d: Expecting payment usually removes Good Samaritan protection.

options.a: A parent or guardian usually consents, with exceptions
options.b: Minors age 16 and older may consent to any care
options.c: School nurses can consent for any student's routine care
options.d: Any minor may consent alone to any surgery

distractorExplanations.b: There is no general age-16 rule; minors consent alone only under specific state exceptions like emancipation.
distractorExplanations.c: School staff, including nurses, cannot give general medical consent in place of a parent or guardian.
distractorExplanations.d: Minors consent alone only under specific state exceptions, such as emancipation.

options.a: Written after the manager decides who was at fault
options.b: Copied into the patient's medical record
options.c: Factual, prompt, and filed per facility policy
options.d: Completed only if the patient was harmed

distractorExplanations.a: Incident reports are written promptly and objectively; assigning fault is not part of the report or a precondition.
distractorExplanations.b: Incident reports are kept separate from the chart; the record notes only the facts of care.
distractorExplanations.d: Near misses and events without harm should also be reported.

options.a: Withholding risks so the patient agrees to treatment
options.b: Respecting a capacitated patient's informed decisions
options.c: Doing what most benefits the patient, as the provider sees it
options.d: Forcing treatment despite informed refusal when the patient has capacity

distractorExplanations.a: Withholding risks to gain agreement is paternalism and defeats informed consent, the opposite of autonomy.
distractorExplanations.c: Acting on the provider's view of the patient's good describes beneficence (or paternalism), not autonomy.
distractorExplanations.d: Forcing care against capacitated refusal violates autonomy.

options.a: Hear risks, benefits, and alternatives, then agree
options.b: Sign the form before any explanation is given
options.c: Agree after the provider decides for them
options.d: Be told the benefits and the provider's recommendation

distractorExplanations.d: Benefits and a recommendation are not enough; risks and alternatives must also be disclosed before consent.
distractorExplanations.b: Signing without explanation is not informed consent.
distractorExplanations.c: Consent must be the patient's voluntary decision.

options.a: Provide training, PPE, and an exposure control plan
options.b: Test exposed employees for HIV and hepatitis every year
options.c: Require staff to buy their own gloves and gowns
options.d: Offer hepatitis C vaccine to all employees

distractorExplanations.b: The standard requires post-exposure evaluation and follow-up, not routine yearly HIV or hepatitis testing of staff.
distractorExplanations.c: Employers must provide PPE at no cost to employees.
distractorExplanations.d: There is no hepatitis C vaccine; employers must offer the hepatitis B vaccine.

options.a: Independently diagnose disease and prescribe medication
options.b: Give injections delegated by the supervising provider
options.c: Perform CLIA-waived tests if trained and authorized
options.d: Take vital signs under supervision/protocol

distractorExplanations.b: Giving injections under provider delegation is within trained MA scope in most states, so it is permitted.
distractorExplanations.c: CLIA-waived testing is often within trained MA scope.
distractorExplanations.d: Vitals are common MA duties.

options.a: A successful treatment outcome
options.b: Following evidence-based protocols perfectly
options.c: Failure to meet the standard of care causing harm
options.d: Intentional touching of a patient without consent

distractorExplanations.d: Intentional unauthorized touching is battery, an intentional tort; negligence is an unintentional breach of duty.
distractorExplanations.a: Good outcomes are not negligence.
distractorExplanations.b: Meeting standards helps prevent negligence claims.

options.a: Names a person to make health decisions for the patient
options.b: Gives someone control over bank accounts
options.c: States treatment wishes if unable to communicate
options.d: Records the patient's organ donor status only

distractorExplanations.a: Naming a decision-maker is done with a health care proxy or durable power of attorney for health care, not a living will.
distractorExplanations.b: Control over finances is a financial power of attorney.
distractorExplanations.d: Organ donation uses a separate registry or document.

options.a: Posting a patient's diagnosis on social media
options.b: Discussing a case with the care team for treatment
options.c: Verifying identity before releasing results
options.d: Faxing records to a specialist for treatment

distractorExplanations.d: HIPAA permits sharing PHI with another provider for treatment, so sending records to a specialist is allowed.
distractorExplanations.b: Treatment-related sharing with the care team is permitted.
distractorExplanations.c: Identity verification protects against wrongful disclosure.

options.a: So complex only a pathologist may run it
options.b: Simple and low-risk if directions are followed
options.c: Not allowed in physician office labs
options.d: Restricted to CLIA-certified reference laboratories

distractorExplanations.d: Waived tests need only a Certificate of Waiver and are routinely run in physician office labs, not reference labs.
distractorExplanations.a: High-complexity tests need qualified lab personnel; waived tests are the simplest category.
distractorExplanations.c: Waived tests are commonly done in physician offices.
